chapter: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
title: Blanton's tone and the microphone problem
summary: Brown laments that early miking never captured Blanton's true tone and compares it to Ray Brown.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: And Blanton changed a lot of things around, did he not?

Well he changed -- yes. It's too bad. I've always regretted that they never got the true tone with Blanton because in those days they didn't put the mike down near the soundpost in the bass fiddle. The mikes all were up in the air on the fingerboard, Well, if you know fingerboard is very tinny upside -- the real true tone, down near the soundpost. So actually they have never heard Jimmy Blanton because he was gone by the time they began to move the mikes around.
Can you describe Blanton's sound as compared to what we hear on records?

Well, it's -- it's richer than the fender-bass, much richer. A very mellow sound. I'll tell you there's one bass player around that gets a similar sound, I can't -- I wouldn't say, whether it's a -- how much better it is or lesser it is, anything like that -- is Ray Brown. Out at the studios. He gets a very good sound and he to me is very reminiscent of Blanton and his work.
Did you hear the album that he and Duke made for Norman Granz (inaudible), called, 'This One's For Blanton.'?
He made that just before Duke died.
Oh, yeah, no I haven't heard that yet.
